# SK2015 — `throw ex;` resets the stack trace

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

Re-throwing the caught exception by name restarts its stack trace at the `throw`.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Syntax |
| Needs a compilation | no |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 0.8 |
| ReSharper | `PossibleIntendedRethrow` (`resharper_possible_intended_rethrow_highlighting`) |

## Why

`throw ex;` inside `catch (Exception ex)` assigns a fresh stack trace to the exception, so every frame between the original throw site and this `catch` is erased. The result is a production log that points at the handler rather than at the fault, which is the one piece of information the log existed to carry. `throw;` re-throws the same exception with its trace intact. The two forms look interchangeable and are not, which is why this is worth a rule rather than a review comment.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
try {
    Parse(input);
} catch (FormatException ex) {
    Log(ex);
    throw ex;
}
```

Write:

```csharp
try {
    Parse(input);
} catch (FormatException ex) {
    Log(ex);
    throw;
}
```

## When it does not fire

The rule fires only when the thrown expression is a bare identifier whose name is the identifier the *nearest enclosing* catch clause declares, and that name is never assigned anywhere inside the clause. Throwing a different exception, a wrapped exception, an exception belonging to an outer catch clause, a field, a parameter, or a variable the clause reassigned is not this pattern and is not reported. `throw ex;` inside a lambda, a local function or a nested catch clause within the block is excluded, because a bare `throw;` is either illegal or means something else there.

- `dotnet_diagnostic.SK2015.severity`
